text:
Turning HTML into markdown
A downloaded page is mostly markup that a reader does not need: navigation bars, scripts, styles and advertisements. to_md strips that away and returns the text as markdown. It accepts either a raw HTML string or a response returned by fetch, and with sel it converts only the part of the page that matches a CSS selector, such as sel='article'. html2md does the same for a string alone, and html_title returns a document’s title.


source

to_md
def to_md(
    res_or_html, # Page dict (from fetch/crawl) or raw HTML string
    sel:str=None, # CSS selector to extract before conversion; returns '' if no match
    multi:bool=False, # Return all selector matches joined
    wrap_tag:str=None, # Wrap each multi-result in <wrap_tag>...</wrap_tag>; only used when multi=True
    ignore_links:bool=True, ignore_images:bool=False,
    readability:bool=True, # False keeps the whole document, for local files and saved pages
)->str:
Convert a response from fetch or an HTML string to markdown, optionally keeping only the parts that match a CSS selector.




source

html2md
def html2md(
    s:str, ignore_links:bool=True, ignore_images:bool=False,
    readability:bool=True, # Extract the article (right for fetched pages); False converts the whole document
):
Convert the HTML string s to markdown, keeping only the main article unless readability=False.




source

html_title
def html_title(
    s:str
)->str:
Return the text of the document’s <title>, or of its first <h1> when it has no title, or an empty string.


By default to_md and html2md run readability, the article extractor behind browser reading modes. It finds the main article and drops everything around it, which is what you want for a page fetched from the web. It can also drop parts of a document you meant to keep, such as section headings. For a page someone saved on purpose, or a local HTML file, pass readability=False. The whole document is then converted, and only scripts, styles, noscript and template blocks and HTML comments are removed. The test below shows readability losing two <h3> headings that readability=False keeps.

title: core
text:
Downloading pages

Refusing private addresses
A program that fetches URLs chosen by an AI agent can be made to fetch addresses inside your own network. Examples are a router’s admin page and a cloud server’s metadata service, which hands out credentials. This attack is called server-side request forgery. check_url refuses any URL that is not http or https. It refuses host names such as localhost and metadata.google.internal. It refuses any host that resolves to a private, loopback, link-local or other non-public address. It raises BlockedURL. The message names two ways to allow such a URL. Pass allow_private=True to one call, or set the environment variable FOSSICK_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1 for the whole process. get_page, fetch, http_get and http_post run this check first. http_page does not.
The check looks up the host name, and then the download looks it up again. The two lookups can get different answers. A person who controls the DNS for a name can give a public address to the check and 127.0.0.1 to the download. This attack is called DNS rebinding. To stop it, the plain HTTP path of get_page gives libcurl the addresses that the check approved, with the libcurl option CURLOPT_RESOLVE. libcurl then connects only to those addresses and does not look up the name again. The plain path also follows redirects itself. Before it connects to a new URL, it checks and pins the address of that URL in the same way. It does not send cookies, auth or credential headers that you supplied to a different host.
Some paths cannot pin the address, and keep only the first check. Through a proxy, also one that is set in the environment, the proxy looks up the name. The browser paths (heavy, stealthy, session, and auto=True after the plain step) check only the first URL. The browser does its own lookups, follows redirects, and loads scripts and images from other addresses with no check. For URLs that you do not trust, use the plain path.


source

check_url
def check_url(
    url:str, # the URL about to be fetched
    allow_private:bool=None, # True skips the check; None skips it only when FOSSICK_ALLOW_PRIVATE is 1, true, yes or on
)->str:
Return url unchanged when it is safe to fetch, or raise BlockedURL when it is not http or https or its host is private or reserved.




source

BlockedURL
def BlockedURL(
    *args, **kwargs
):
The error raised when a URL points at a private, local or cloud metadata address.




Downloading one page
get_page runs check_url, then downloads the page in one of four ways. By default it sends a plain HTTP request. heavy=True loads the page in a headless browser so that its JavaScript runs. stealthy=True uses scrapling’s stealth browser, which is built to pass bot checks such as Cloudflare’s. session=True uses the logged-in Chrome described in fossick.cdp, with its cookies. The browsers load on first use. When they cannot load, get_page raises BrowserUnavailable.
http_get and http_post are get_page with the method set and a 30 second timeout. All of them verify TLS certificates by default. Pass verify=False only for a host you trust that has a bad certificate. http_page sends a plain request with GET, POST, PUT or DELETE and skips the address check. Use http_page only for URLs your own code chose. Most callers need fetch, below.
Two optional limits apply to the plain path. max_bytes stops the download when the body becomes larger than that number of bytes, and raises TooLarge. A server that sends gigabytes then cannot fill the memory before to_md runs. max_recv_speed sets the highest download speed, in bytes per second. Both limits are off by default. The browser paths do not use them. http_page also takes max_bytes, and curl_options for other libcurl options.
Some networks inspect TLS traffic with their own root certificate. curl_cffi does not use the system keychain, so on such a machine a check of the certificate fails with curl: (60) ... unable to get local issuer certificate. Give the plain path a CA bundle file that holds the normal roots and the inspection root. Pass ca_bundle= or verify= with the path of the file, or set one of the environment variables SSL_CERT_FILE, CURL_CA_BUNDLE or REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE. fossick reads them in that order, on each request. It uses the first one that names a file. On macOS, when none of these is set, fossick uses the system keychain. It reads the certificates of the system keychains once with security find-certificate, adds them to certifi’s roots, and keeps the result in its cache folder for one day. An inspection root that your company put in the system keychain then works with no setup. The bundle applies only when verification is on: with verify=True, as http_get sets it, or with ca_bundle=. fossick never turns verification off. On other systems, when none of these is set, nothing changes.

source

r1=get_page('https://httpbin.org/get', verify=False)
r1.__dict__.keys()


from fastcore.test import test_fail


try: get_page('https://httpbin.org/put', method='PUT', verify=False)
except AssertionError as e: test_fail(str(e) == 'Only GET and POST methods are supported')


http_page('https://httpbin.org/put', method='PUT', verify=False).status



fetch
Most code downloads a page with fetch. It wraps get_page and returns scrapling’s response object with two attributes added. html holds the page, or only the part matching sel. xhr holds the background requests recorded when capture_xhr=True. The response also has status, url, and a json() method for JSON replies.
auto=True tries the download methods in turn: plain HTTP, then the headless browser, then the stealth browser, then the stealth browser through the logged-in Chrome. A bot wall is a page that asks for a verification step instead of showing the requested content. auto=True stops at the first response that is not a bot wall. It records the method that worked in tier, or 'blocked' if none did. It records each failed attempt and its reason in errs.
browser_session downloads many pages with one browser. Starting a browser takes seconds. browser_session opens one browser for the length of a with block and gives you a fetch-like function that reuses it.
auto=True can end in the logged-in Chrome. That last method connects to the debug Chrome on port 9223, starts it if it is not running, and sends the cookies that Chrome has for the site. This is correct for a page that you want to read as yourself. It is not correct for a URL that comes from a web page, a document or another person. Such a URL can make your logged-in browser open a page with your cookies. When you do not trust the URL, pass auto=False. This is the default for fetch, but not for read. With auto=False, and without heavy, stealthy, session or capture_xhr, no function in this module starts a browser or connects to port 9223. This includes get_pdf and its proof-of-work step, read_arxiv, read_gh_file, crawl and read. The plain path always checks redirects: follow_redirects is 'safe' by default, and fossick checks and pins each step itself. The section Fetching untrusted URLs, near the end of this notebook, tests this.


source

browser_session
def browser_session(
    stealthy:bool=False, headless:bool=True, **init_kw
):
Keep one browser open for a with block and yield a fetch(url, sel=None) function that reuses it.




source

fetch
def fetch(
    url:str, # URL to fetch
    sel:str=None, # CSS selector to extract (None = full page)
    method:str='GET', # HTTP method; 'POST' sends payload as JSON body
    payload:dict=None, # POST body (JSON) or GET query params
    heavy:bool=False, # Full JS rendering via headless browser
    stealthy:bool=False, # Anti-bot stealth fetcher (Cloudflare etc.)
    capture_xhr:bool=False, # Capture XHR calls made by the page (only works with heavy or stealthy)
    session:bool=False, # Route through the persistent debug Chrome (reuses its logged-in cookies); True or a port int
    auto:bool=False, # Try plain, heavy, stealthy, then the logged-in debug Chrome with its cookies for the site; keep False for untrusted URLs
    allow_private:bool=None, # Allow localhost/intranet targets (default: refuse; $FOSSICK_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1)
    max_bytes:int=None, # Plain HTTP only: raise `TooLarge` when the body is larger than this many bytes (default: no limit)
    max_recv_speed:int=None, # Plain HTTP only: the highest download speed, in bytes per second (default: no limit)
    **kw
)->scrapling.engines.toolbelt.custom.Response: # Extra kwargs passed to scrapling (e.g. verify, headers, timeout)
Download url and return the response with .html set to the page, or the part matching sel, and .xhr set to any recorded background requests. auto=True can end in the logged-in debug Chrome, so pass auto=False for untrusted URLs.




Bot walls
Many sites put a challenge page in front of their content for visitors they think are scripts. Cloudflare’s “Just a moment” page and the Anubis proof-of-work page are common examples. The challenge often arrives with status 200, so it looks like a successful download. fossick treats a response as blocked when its status is 401, 403, 429, 503 or 530, when its HTML contains the marker of a known challenge or captcha widget, or when it is a 200 response with less than 200 characters of HTML. The tests below check these rules, including that a page which only mentions the word captcha is not counted as blocked.
The cells after that run against real sites and are not run by the tests. They show a Cloudflare and an Anubis wall being detected, auto=True stopping at the plain tier for a page that needs nothing more, browser_session reusing one browser for two pages, and session=True going through the logged-in Chrome.

# A site behind Cloudflare: a plain fetch hits the bot wall, and _blocked() flags it for escalation
cf = fetch('https://www.scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge', verify=False)
assert cf.status == 403, f'expected a Cloudflare 403 challenge, got {cf.status}'
assert _blocked(cf) is True            # fetch(auto=True) escalates from here (heavy -> stealthy -> session)
print('cloudflare:', cf.status, '| blocked?', _blocked(cf))


# A site behind Anubis (proof-of-work bot wall): _blocked() now recognizes it, so fetch(auto=True) escalates
an = fetch('https://anubis.techaro.lol/', verify=False)
assert 'making sure' in an.html.lower(), 'expected the Anubis challenge page'
assert _blocked(an) is True            # Anubis markers are in _BLOCK_MARKERS -> auto escalates past this wall
print('anubis wall detected by _blocked?', _blocked(an))


# regression: a normal page that merely *mentions* captcha must NOT read as a bot wall.
# Wikipedia embeds hCaptcha config keys in its page JS -- the word is there, but there's no challenge widget.
wiki = fetch('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anubis', verify=False)
assert wiki.status == 200 and 'captcha' in wiki.html.lower()   # the word IS present on the page...
assert _blocked(wiki) is False   # ...but _BLOCK_MARKERS matches captcha *widgets* (g-recaptcha/h-captcha/...), not the word


# fetch(auto=True): walks plain->heavy->stealthy->session, stops at the first unblocked tier, tags .tier
plain = fetch('https://example.com', auto=True, verify=False)
assert plain.status == 200 and plain.tier == 'plain'   # a static page needs no escalation
print('example.com ->', plain.tier)


# browser_session(): open ONE browser, reuse it across fetches (skips per-URL relaunch)
with browser_session() as bf:
    a = bf('https://example.com')
    b = bf('https://httpbin.org/html')
assert a.status == 200 and b.status == 200
assert len(a.html) > 0 and len(b.html) > 0


# fetch(session=True): route through the persistent debug Chrome, reusing its logged-in cookies
pg = fetch('https://httpbin.org/headers', session=True)
assert pg.status == 200
print(pg.html[:200])

text:
Crawling and batches
crawl visits pages breadth-first, starting from one URL and following the links that match follow_sel, until it has visited max_pages pages. By default it stays on the starting site. It returns the responses that came back with status 200, and a page that fails to download is reported and skipped. delay waits between requests so as not to load a small site heavily. For crawls with heavy or stealthy, one browser is kept open for the whole crawl unless reuse=False.


source

crawl
def crawl(
    start_url:str, # URL to start from
    sel:str=None, # CSS selector to extract per page
    follow_sel:str='a[href]', # CSS selector for links to follow
    same_domain:bool=True, # Only follow links on same domain
    max_pages:int=10, # Max pages to visit
    delay:float=0, # Seconds to wait between requests (polite crawling)
    heavy:bool=False, # Full JS rendering via headless browser
    stealthy:bool=False, # Anti-bot stealth fetcher (Cloudflare etc.)
    reuse:bool=True, # For heavy/stealthy crawls, keep one browser open across pages
    **kw
)->list: # Extra kwargs passed to scrapling (e.g. verify, timeout)
Visit pages breadth-first from start_url, following links that match follow_sel, and return the responses that had status 200.


fetch_all downloads a list of URLs you already have, in parallel threads, and returns the responses in the same order. get_options reads the choices out of a <select> drop-down, which is how many sites list chapters, categories or years; the example uses a small page with three options.

Return the options of the <select> element matched by sel as a list of {'value', 'text'} dictionaries.

text:
PDFs and arXiv papers
get_pdf downloads a PDF, or reads one from disk, and returns it as a PdfDocument from pdf_oxide, or None when the bytes are not a PDF. It checks for the %PDF- signature in the first 1024 bytes of the content and ignores the URL. arXiv serves papers from URLs with no .pdf ending. The NCBI PubMed Central archive puts a small proof-of-work check in front of its PDFs. When the reply is such a check, get_pdf solves it and downloads the PDF again with the answer. Any page can contain the markers of this check, so the second download goes through the plain path of get_page, with the same address and redirect checks, timeout and max_bytes as the first. max_bytes limits the size of the PDF. When save_path is a folder or a file name, it saves a copy of the file. The examples download two papers from the Self-Determination Theory site and print the start of their text.


source

get_pdf
def get_pdf(
    url_or_path:str, # URL or local path to PDF
    save_path:NoneType=None, # optional path to save the PDF (directory or full path)
    max_bytes:int=None, # raise `TooLarge` when the download is larger than this many bytes (default: no limit)
    **scrapling_kw
)->pdf_oxide.pdf_oxide.PdfDocument | None: # extra kwargs passed to `get_page` (e.g. verify, headers, timeout, allow_private)
Download a PDF from a URL, or read one from disk, and return it as a PdfDocument, or None when the bytes are not a PDF.



import tempfile


sp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())


sdt = 'https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/SDT/documents/2000_RyanDeci_SDT.pdf'
sdt_p = get_pdf(sdt, save_path=sp, verify=False)


sdt_p.to_markdown_all()[:200]


gdr = 'https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/1997_GrolnickDeciRyan.pdf'
gcr = get_pdf(gdr, save_path=sp, verify=False)


gcr.to_markdown_all()[:200]

read_arxiv takes an arXiv URL, of either the abstract page or the PDF, or a bare id such as 2306.14881. It returns the paper’s title, authors, summary, published date, link, pdf_url and pdf_path. By default it also saves the PDF in save_dir. With source=True it adds the full text of the paper as markdown under source. The metadata is cached on disk. A second call for the same paper makes no request. force=True fetches the metadata again.

Return an arXiv paper’s metadata and PDF path, and optionally its full text, caching the metadata on disk.



read_arxiv('https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14881')['summary'][:200]

lookup_doi finds the DOI of a paper from its title by asking Crossref, and returns it as a https://doi.org/ link, or None when Crossref has no match.

Return the doi.org URL of the first Crossref result for title, or None.

These functions turn documents into markdown or notebooks. pdf2md converts a PDF to one markdown string, with pages separated by ---, using pdflite. It saves images from the PDF in an images folder inside a folder named after out_path. This module re-exports pdflite’s own functions, such as pdf_md and clean_md. url2nb saves a web page, PDF or arXiv paper as a Jupyter notebook. pdf2nb saves a PDF as a notebook. Both return the notebook’s path. Both skip the work when the notebook already exists, unless force=True.

from pdf_oxide import Pdf


_c = _md2cells('# Intro\n\nSome prose.\n\n[code]\n\n> 1+1\n2\n[/code]\n\n## Next\n\nMore.')
assert [(c.cell_type, c.source) for c in _c] == [('markdown','# Intro\n\nSome prose.'), ('code','1+1\n# => 2'), ('markdown','## Next\n\nMore.')], _c

try: _hp = url2nb('https://example.com/page', nb_path=_t/'page.ipynb')
finally: fetch = _rf

title: core
text:
GitHub
gh_clone returns a local copy of a repository. The first call clones it into fossick’s cache folder, in a folder named owner__repo. It clones over HTTPS only, and never asks for a password. Pass ssh=True to try SSH after HTTPS, for a private repository and an SSH key. SSH then runs in batch mode, so it fails at once when it needs a passphrase. The clone is shallow: it gets only the latest commit. Pass depth=None for the full history, or a different number of commits. timeout is the time limit for each git command, in seconds. When git takes longer, fossick stops git, removes the part-made folder and raises TimeoutError. Later calls fetch the clone and reset it to the latest commit. Git runs with /dev/null as stdin and never reads the caller’s terminal. fossick gives git its own environment and does not change os.environ. fossick refuses a target that starts with -, and puts -- before the URL, so that git cannot read a URL as an option. gh_clone returns a local path unchanged. Code that accepts a repository therefore accepts a folder on disk. read_gh_repo reads files from that clone and returns {path: text}. By default it reads the README, pyproject.toml and every Python file. It caches its results for an hour. read_gh_file downloads one file as raw text from its GitHub page URL. It returns source code exactly as written. It converts the file to markdown only when GitHub serves HTML.


source

read_gh_file
def read_gh_file(
    url:str, # GitHub blob URL of the file to read
    **kw
):
Return the contents of one file from its GitHub page URL.




source

read_gh_repo
def read_gh_repo(
    path_or_url:str, # GitHub URL, SSH address, or local path
    globs:tuple=None, # file glob patterns (default: README*, pyproject.toml, *.py)
    limit:int=None, # max files to return
    as_list:bool=False, # return list of Paths instead of {path: content} dict
)->dict:
Return the files of a GitHub repository or local folder that match globs, as a {path: text} dictionary.




source

gh_clone
def gh_clone(
    path_or_url:str, # GitHub URL, SSH address, or a local path (returned as-is)
    depth:int=1, # commits of history to clone; None for all of them
    timeout:float=300, # seconds for each git command; then git is stopped and the part-made folder removed
    ssh:bool=False, # try SSH after HTTPS, for a private repo and an SSH key
)->pathlib.Path:
Return a local clone of a GitHub repository, cloned or updated in fossick’s cache, or return a local path unchanged.


These tests give gh_clone a fake subprocess.run, so they need no network. By default the clone is HTTPS only and shallow, and -- comes before the URL. A failed HTTPS clone does not try SSH, because SSH can ask for a passphrase. With ssh=True, SSH comes second and runs in batch mode. Git gets its own environment, and os.environ stays the same. A clone that passes timeout raises TimeoutError and leaves no folder. A target that starts with - is refused before git runs.

from unittest.mock import patch

title: core
section: Finding the API behind a page
text:
Finding the API behind a page
Many modern pages arrive nearly empty. JavaScript then loads their data with background requests, called XHR or fetch calls, which usually return JSON. You can read that JSON directly instead of scraping the rendered page. find_xhr loads a page in a headless browser, records the background requests it makes, and returns each one whose URL matches pattern as a dictionary with url, content_type and the decoded data. With session=True it records the requests through the logged-in Chrome instead, and each result also carries a capture. replay_xhr sends a captured request again as a plain HTTP call with the browser’s cookies. Use it to call an API that needs a login without keeping a browser open.
pattern can be a regular expression, such as .*products.*, or a shell-style glob, such as *products*. compile_pattern accepts both: it tries the text as a regular expression and, when that is invalid, reads it as a glob.


source

replay_xhr
def replay_xhr(
    capture:dict, # a request dict from cdp.calls() or find_xhr(session=True)[i].capture
    data:NoneType=None, # override request body (str/dict); defaults to the captured body
    port:int=9223, # debug Chrome port to pull cookies from
    use_cookies:bool=True, # attach the browser's cookies for this domain (keeps auth)
    **kw
)->scrapling.engines.toolbelt.custom.Response: # Extra kwargs passed to the underlying Fetcher (headers, params, verify)
Send a request captured from the browser again as a plain HTTP call, with the debug Chrome’s cookies for that site.




source

find_xhr
def find_xhr(
    url:str, # URL to visit with browser
    pattern:str='*', # Glob or regex pattern to filter captured XHR URLs
    session:bool=False, # Use the persistent debug Chrome (authenticated) instead of a throwaway browser
    port:int=9223, # debug Chrome port (only when session=True)
    tail:int=3, # seconds to keep listening after navigation (only when session=True)
    **kw
)->list: # Extra kwargs passed to fetch (verify, network_idle, etc.)
Load url in a browser and return the background requests it makes whose URLs match pattern.




source

compile_pattern
def compile_pattern(
    pattern
):
Compile pattern as a regular expression, or as a shell-style glob such as *foo* when it is not a valid one.



assert compile_pattern('.*products.*').search('https://api.example.com/products?q=1')
assert compile_pattern('*products*').search('https://api.example.com/products?q=1')
assert not compile_pattern('*products*').search('https://api.example.com/search')
assert compile_pattern('.*[Ss]earch.*').search('https://api.example.com/Search')

An API rarely returns its records at the top level of the JSON. They might be under results, or several levels down at data.products.items. json_records finds them by searching the whole payload for the longest list of dictionaries, and with_key=True also tells you which key held it.
paginate_api reads every page of a paged JSON API. It sends the request repeatedly, raising the page number in page_field each time, and stops when a page comes back empty or shorter than the page size, or after max_pages pages. It finds each page’s records with results_field if you name one and json_records if you do not. With save=True each page is written to a file, and a later run reads the saved pages instead of fetching them again.

    **kw

Request successive pages of a JSON API and return the items from every page in one list.

text:
YouTube
These three functions use yt-dlp. search_yt searches YouTube and returns a list of result dictionaries. read_yt returns one video’s details and its transcript under the key source. The transcript comes from YouTube’s English automatic captions. A video without them has an empty transcript. read_yt(url, cues=True) adds cues, a list of {start, end, text} with times in seconds, so a caller can seek to a line. yt_link(url, seconds) makes a watch link that opens at that time. read_yt caches results, cues included, on disk by video id. download_yt saves a video’s audio as mp3 or its video as mp4. The mp3 format needs ffmpeg. All three accept verify=False to skip certificate checks. Use it behind a proxy that rewrites HTTPS.

text:
One function for every source
read accepts every kind of target the readers above handle and returns the same seven fields for all of them: ok, kind, title, source, text, skipped and meta. A program can treat web pages, PDFs, arXiv papers, YouTube videos, GitHub content and local files alike.
what_is decides which reader a target needs. A path that exists on disk wins over every URL rule, so a local file named pdf is read from disk rather than fetched. A GitHub URL containing /blob/ is one file (ghfile) rather than a whole repository (github). Any other http or https URL is a web page. A failed read returns ok=False with the reason in skipped. Only a target that is none of these kinds raises ValueError.
what_is reads the host of a URL to find arXiv and YouTube links, not the full text of the URL. https://docs.example.dev/youtube.com-guide is a web page, not a YouTube video.

title: core
text:
Fetching untrusted URLs
A program that reads links from web pages, documents or messages fetches URLs that another person can choose. For these URLs, call fetch, get_pdf and read with auto=False. fossick then uses only plain HTTP. It checks and pins each address, and checks each redirect again. max_bytes can limit the size of each download.
The tests below use a small web server in this process, on 127.0.0.1. The address check refuses 127.0.0.1, so _public_loopback makes the check count it as public for the length of a test. The server can then act as a site on the internet. _public_loopback can also give a name an address that only the check sees. libcurl does not see that address.
Any page can contain the proof-of-work markers that get_pdf looks for. Here the page contains them, and the answer gets a redirect to localhost. get_pdf refuses the redirect. The server log shows that the request to /secret was not sent.

_Site.hits.clear()
with _public_loopback(): test_fail(lambda: get_pdf(f'{_base}/paper.pdf'), contains='localhost is an internal host')
test_eq(_Site.hits, ['/paper.pdf', '/paper.pdf'])   # the answer was sent; the redirect to /secret was not followed

fossick checks a redirect by the address that its host resolves to, not only by its name. Here inside.invalid resolves to 10.0.0.7, so fossick refuses the redirect. The second fetch tests the pin. Names that end in .invalid never resolve in real DNS. The fetch can reach the server only through the address that the check approved and gave to libcurl.

_Site.hits.clear()
with _public_loopback({'inside.invalid': '10.0.0.7'}):
    test_fail(lambda: fetch(f'{_base}/to-inside'), contains='resolves to 10.0.0.7')
with _public_loopback({'pinned.invalid': '127.0.0.1'}):
    r = fetch(f'http://pinned.invalid:{_srv.server_port}/page')
test_eq(r.status, 200)
test_eq(_Site.hits, ['/to-inside', '/page'])

max_bytes stops a large body. The server sends 4 MB with no Content-Length. fetch and get_pdf stop after 100,000 bytes and raise TooLarge. With no max_bytes, the download is not limited, as before.

test_fail(lambda: fetch(f'{_base}/big', allow_private=True, max_bytes=100_000, retries=1), contains='max_bytes=100000')
test_fail(lambda: get_pdf(f'{_base}/big', allow_private=True, max_bytes=100_000, retries=1), contains='max_bytes=100000')
with _public_loopback(): test_fail(lambda: fetch(f'{_base}/big', max_bytes=100_000, retries=1), contains='max_bytes')
test_eq(len(fetch(f'{_base}/big', allow_private=True).body), 64 * 65536)   # no limit unless one is asked for

A CA bundle from SSL_CERT_FILE is used on each request. The test starts an HTTPS server with a self-signed certificate, made with the openssl command. Without the bundle, the certificate check fails. With SSL_CERT_FILE set to the certificate, or with ca_bundle=, the download works. verify=True stays on in each case.

import ssl, tempfile
_td = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
subprocess.run(['openssl', 'req', '-x509', '-newkey', 'rsa:2048', '-nodes', '-days', '1', '-subj', '/CN=127.0.0.1',
                '-addext', 'subjectAltName=IP:127.0.0.1', '-keyout', str(_td/'key.pem'), '-out', str(_td/'cert.pem')],
               check=True, capture_output=True, stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL)
_tls = ThreadingHTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 0), _Site)
_ctx = ssl.create_default_context(ssl.Purpose.CLIENT_AUTH); _ctx.load_cert_chain(_td/'cert.pem', _td/'key.pem')
_tls.socket = _ctx.wrap_socket(_tls.socket, server_side=True)
threading.Thread(target=_tls.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
_https = f'https://127.0.0.1:{_tls.server_port}/notes.txt'

_env = {v: os.environ.pop(v) for v in ('SSL_CERT_FILE', 'CURL_CA_BUNDLE', 'REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE') if v in os.environ}
try:
    test_fail(lambda: http_get(_https, allow_private=True, retries=1), contains='(60)')
    test_eq(http_get(_https, allow_private=True, retries=1, ca_bundle=_td/'cert.pem').body, b'secret')
    os.environ['SSL_CERT_FILE'] = str(_td/'cert.pem')
    test_eq(http_get(_https, allow_private=True, retries=1).body, b'secret')
    with _public_loopback(): test_eq(fetch(_https, verify=True, retries=1).body, b'secret')   # the pinned path too
finally:
    os.environ.pop('SSL_CERT_FILE', None); os.environ.update(_env)
    _tls.shutdown(); _tls.server_close()

On macOS, _system_ca makes the CA bundle from certifi’s roots and the output of security find-certificate. The first test gives it a fake security command, so it runs on every system. The bundle holds the certifi roots and the fake certificate. A fresh file is used again without a new security call. When security gives no certificate, _system_ca keeps the old file. Off macOS, _system_ca returns None and curl uses its own roots.

from unittest.mock import patch
import certifi, tempfile


_fake_pem = '-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\nZmFrZQ==\n-----END CERTIFICATE-----\n'
_calls = []
def _fake_run(cmd, **kw):
    _calls.append(cmd)

Checkout forms
shop_fields lists every visible form field on the page. Each entry has the field number i, the label, the autocomplete token and the current value. A drop-down entry also lists its options. shop_fields never returns password values.
shop_fill fills a form from a profile dictionary. The standard keys are first_name, last_name, email, phone, address1, address2, city, state, postcode, country, company, notes and the card_* keys. match_fields decides which field each key goes into. It checks the field’s autocomplete token first, then its name or id, then its label. It uses the words in FIELD_MAP, which include Australian wording such as “suburb” and “postcode”. Each field is used for one key at most.
A numeric key, such as '7', fills field number 7 from shop_fields. Use it for choices that have no standard key, such as size or delivery time.
After the fill, shop_fill reads the form again and reports whether each field holds the value. shop_set sets one field by its number.
shop_fill(submit=...) clicks a button or link by its name after the fill. A name that matches PAY_RX, such as “Pay now” or “Place order”, needs confirm=True. Without it, shop_fill raises ShopError and fills nothing.

title: quality
text:
A search engine ranks pages by how well they match a query. That is not the same as how worth reading they are. A question about building rules in Australia can return five cost guides from one trade directory ahead of the government page that sets the rules. A programming question can return sites that copy Stack Overflow answers.
This module reorders results before any page is downloaded. It does these things:
research in fossick.search calls curate when curated=True, its default. It also uses plan and interleave. Each function here also works on its own, on any list of result dictionaries with an href or url.

section: Which site a URL belongs to
text:
Which site a URL belongs to
Two URLs belong to the same site when they share a registrable domain, the part of the name someone registered: docs.python.org and www.python.org both belong to python.org. Usually that is the last two parts of the host name. In countries whose registries sell names one level down, such as bbc.co.uk or nsw.gov.au, it is the last three. MULTI_LABEL_SUFFIXES lists those registry endings for the countries fossick handles. host returns a URL’s host name in lower case without www., and registrable_domain returns the site.

title: quality

One key per page
The same page often appears under several URLs: with and without www., with a trailing slash, or with tracking parameters such as utm_source added by whoever shared it. norm_url reduces a URL to one key. It drops the scheme, the www., the fragment, tracking parameters, a default port and a trailing slash. It sorts the query parameters. A port that is not the default stays in the key. interleave, cluster_sources and diversity use the key to decide when two results are the same page.

title: quality
text:
Authority depends on the question
The source to trust depends on the question. For a question about the law, a government site is the authority. For a question about a library, its documentation is. For a question about what users think, a forum is. DOMAIN_RULES lists, for each kind of question, the sites to move up (boost) and the sites to move down (demote). The kinds are docs, policy, release, security and community.
domain_matches checks one host name against one rule. A rule has one of four forms:








Rule
Matches
Example




Ends in a dot
Host names that start with it
docs.


Starts with a dot
The ending itself and every host under it
.gov.au


Contains a /
Only the host name before the /, with no subdomains
github.com/advisories


Any other text
That domain and its subdomains
sec.gov



Only a rule that ends in a dot matches the start of a host name. openai.com.evil.example does not match openai.com. blocked_matches applies the last form, the domain and its subdomains, to a blocked list.

    domain:str, rule:str
)->bool:
Return True when domain is the domain rule or one of its subdomains.

section: How many stories, not how many URLs
text:
How many stories, not how many URLs
Ten results can be one story, for example a news agency report that nine sites reprinted. cluster_sources groups results that have the same norm_url key or that share most of their text.
shingles returns the set of three-word sequences in a text. jaccard divides the size of the overlap of two sets by the size of their union. cluster_sources applies jaccard to the shingles of each result’s title and text. Two results with a similarity at or above threshold (0.6 by default) are one story. The grouping is transitive. When A matches B and B matches C, all three are one group. Each group is named after its first member in the input order.
independence returns the groups with a score. The score rises with the number of separate stories and the number of separate sites. The result also lists its limits. Two sites that rewrite one press release in their own words do not share enough text to be grouped.

title: fossick
text:
fossick gets text off the web and into a program. You give it a search query, a URL, an arXiv id, a YouTube link, a GitHub repository or a local file. It gives back markdown that a person or a language model can read. It was written for AI agents that look things up. Its functions return plain data (strings, lists and dictionaries) that you can print or pass to a model as they are.
The library works in layers. search sends a query to several search engines at once and merges their answers into one ranked list. read takes a single target and returns its text. Under read, fetch downloads a page and to_md turns its HTML into markdown. Many sites refuse plain downloads from scripts. fetch can also load a page in a headless browser, in a stealth browser built to pass bot checks, or in a copy of Chrome you have logged in to. For pages that need clicking and typing, cdp_connect drives that Chrome directly. Everything here is also available from the shell as the fossick command and as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that agents can call.

assert '# fossick' in result.text and result.skipped is None
result.kind, result.title, result.ok

A folder or a GitHub repository is a tree of files, not one document. read does not turn it into text. It returns ok=True with an empty text and the local path in meta['path']. The caller chooses which files to open. For a GitHub repository, that path is a fresh clone in fossick’s cache. With pages=True, a PDF returns a list of (page_index, text) pairs. Page indexes start at 0.
Sometimes a target is recognised but yields nothing: a site serves a bot check instead of the page, a YouTube video has no English captions, or a URL that looked like a PDF returns something else. read reports these with ok=False and a reason in skipped, and does not raise. It raises ValueError only when the target is none of the kinds above.

title: fossick
text:
A logged-in Chrome
Some pages are only shown to a logged-in user. fossick reaches them through a separate copy of Chrome that runs with remote debugging switched on, on port 9223, with its own profile in ~/.cache/fastcdp/cdp-chrome. cdp_connect starts it the first time it is needed. Log in to a site once in that window. The cookies stay in the profile. Later calls such as fetch(url, session=True) then use the logged-in session. fetch(url, auto=True) and read fall back to this Chrome when every other method is blocked.
To start it by hand in a visible window, for logging in, run await cdp_setup(headless=False). The fastcdp-setup command, installed with fossick’s fastcdp dependency, adds a launcher for the same Chrome and profile to your applications.

title: fossick
text:
Untrusted URLs
fetch(url, auto=True) and read, which uses auto=True by default, can end in the logged-in Chrome on port 9223. That step starts the Chrome if it is not running and sends the cookies it has for the site. Use it only for URLs that you chose. When a URL comes from a web page, a document or another person, pass auto=False:
fetch(url, auto=False, max_bytes=20_000_000)   # plain HTTP only; stop after 20 MB
read(url, auto=False, max_bytes=20_000_000)    # also for PDFs, arXiv papers and GitHub files
With auto=False, fossick does not start a browser or connect to port 9223, also for PDFs and the redirects that a page sends. The plain path refuses private and local addresses. It connects only to the address that it checked, so a second DNS answer cannot send it to 127.0.0.1. It checks each redirect in the same way. max_bytes and max_recv_speed limit the size and speed of a download. Both are off by default. Through a proxy, and in the browser paths, fossick checks only the first URL.
On a machine that inspects TLS traffic with its own root certificate, curl_cffi does not trust that root, because it does not use the system keychain. A download then fails with curl: (60) ... unable to get local issuer certificate. Set SSL_CERT_FILE to a CA bundle file that holds the normal roots and the inspection root, for example export SSL_CERT_FILE=~/Library/Java/macos-all-ca.pem. fossick also reads CURL_CA_BUNDLE and REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, and takes ca_bundle= on each call. Verification stays on.

title: mcp
text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way for an AI agent, such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, to discover and call tools that run outside it. This module offers fossick’s functions as MCP tools. The agent sees each tool’s name, arguments and docstring. The docstrings here are written for the agent and say when to use each option. They are the tools’ interface, and they are longer than the docstrings elsewhere in fossick.
Most tools take the arguments of the Python function they wrap, plus a limit on how much text they return, such as max_chars. A tool cuts a long result at that limit and ends it with a note that gives the number of characters cut. The note tells an agent to ask for more. Tools convert results to plain JSON types before they return them. The server uses standard input and output by default.

title: search
text:
search asks several search engines the same question at once and merges their answers into one list. Each engine misses pages the others find, and a page that several engines rank highly is usually a good one. fossick reaches the engines through ddgs, which needs no API keys. It merges the lists with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), explained below. It can then reorder the merged list by how well each result matches the query.
google gets Google’s own ranking by loading the results page in a stealth browser. It is slower than search. research searches, downloads the best results that have readable text, and returns them as one markdown digest that cites each source. You can pass the digest to a language model as it is.

Asking each engine
For text search, fossick queries each engine in TEXT_BACKENDS separately and keeps each engine’s results in the order that engine ranked them. It does not use ddgs’s own combined search, which picks engines at random and favours Wikipedia. backends lists every engine ddgs offers for a category. With pages above 1, fossick asks each engine for that many pages of results, and drops results on later pages that repeat earlier ones. title: search
text:
Merging the lists
Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists without needing the engines’ own scores, which are not comparable. Each page gets 1/(k + rank) from every list it appears in, and those amounts are added up. A page ranked first by one engine scores more than a page ranked eighth, and a page found by several engines adds up a score from each. k, 60 by default, controls how much more the top ranks count than the lower ones.
rrf treats two URLs as the same page when they differ only in scheme, www., a trailing slash or tracking parameters, using norm_url from fossick.quality. For each page it keeps the longest snippet any engine gave, the fused score, and engines, the list of engines that found it.

title: search
text:
Reranking
Search engines rank by many things besides relevance to the exact words asked. rerank reorders results by how well their title, snippet and URL match the query. It blends that score with the merged score. mix is the weight of the merged score. The default is 0.4. At 1 the reranker is ignored. When method is not 'none', rerank adds a rerank field with the relevance score to each result.
method chooses the scorer. 'lexical' uses BM25, a standard word-matching formula. bm25 computes scores from the result list. It needs no stored index. 'flashrank' uses the small cross-encoder model of flashrank. The model reads the query and each result together and matches meaning better. It needs pip install flashrank. flashrank_scores returns None when flashrank is missing, and method='flashrank' then raises ImportError. 'auto' uses flashrank when installed and BM25 otherwise. 'none', the default for search, keeps the merged order.

Where and when
The best answer to many questions depends on the country. Building rules, prices and what is for sale all differ. Search engines take a region code of the form country-language, such as au-en. With region='auto', the default, fossick works out the two halves separately from the query.
infer_country looks for country names, adjectives and big cities from COUNTRY_WORDS. It answers only when the query names exactly one country. A query that names two countries gets None. infer_language counts common function words from LANG_WORDS, such as “the” and “what” or “der” and “und”. It answers only when one language has the most matches and has at least two. infer_region joins the two results. A query that names no language takes the usual language of the country it names, from COUNTRY_LANG. The default us-en fills whatever the query leaves open. An English question about France gives fr-en.
timelimit keeps only recent results: 'd', 'w', 'm' or 'y' for the past day, week, month or year.

title: search
text:
research
research turns a question into a set of readable sources in these steps:

plan, from fossick.quality, splits a question that asks several things into one search per part, and keeps the original question as the first search.
Each search runs with search, or with google when engine='google'. It interleaves their results, taking one from each in turn. Each part of the question gets sources.
With curated=True, the default, curate removes sites that copy other sites’ content and moves authoritative sources up. research drops copycats before it downloads any page.
It downloads the candidates in order with fetch(auto=True). Each batch has as many pages as n still lacks. It stops when it has n pages with at least 400 characters of readable markdown. A page that failed, was blocked, or was too short goes into dropped with its reason. The next candidate takes its place.
With focused=True, focus cuts each page down to about chars characters of the passages that best answer the question.

It returns a dictionary with the query, the sources, the digest, the dropped pages, the region it used, the curation report and the plan. Each source holds its title, href, the fetch tier that worked, its publication date, the queries it answered and its markdown in md. The digest joins the sources, separated by ---, each headed by its title, URL, publication date when known, and the part of the question it answers.
Three helpers work on their own. page_date finds the date a page says it was published and returns it as YYYY-MM-DD, or None. It reads the JSON-LD data, the <meta> tags (the names in DATE_META), a <time> element, or a /2018/09/ style URL. usable checks that a fetched page is a 200 response, is not a bot wall, and has at least min_chars characters of readable markdown. min_chars=0 skips the length check. focus keeps the parts of a long page that answer a query. It keeps the opening blocks up to 30% of the budget, because reference pages often answer in their first paragraphs. It then adds the blocks that score best for the query. It returns them in their original order with … marking the gaps.
The cell below this one tests paging with stand-in engines.

def _fake(be, q, region='us-en', page=1, timeout=8, tries=2, **kw):
    _seen.append((be, page))
    start = (page-1)*2
    return [dict(title=f'{be}{i}', href=f'https://e.com/{be}/{i}', body='', engine=be, rank=i-start+1)
            for i in range(start, start+3)]        # 3 hits/page, overlapping the next page by one
_real, _engine_hits = _engine_hits, _fake
try:
    one = _backend_lists('q', ('brave',), pages=1)
    two = _backend_lists('q', ('brave',), pages=2)
    later = _backend_lists('q', ('brave',), page=3)
finally: _engine_hits = _real

assert sorted(_seen[:3]) == [('brave',1), ('brave',1), ('brave',2)], _seen   # one job per (backend, page)
assert _seen[3:] == [('brave',3)]                                        # `page` is where paging starts
assert len(one[0]) == 3 and len(two[0]) == 5                             # 3+3 minus the one repeat
assert [h['rank'] for h in two[0]] == [1,2,3,4,5]                        # continuous, not 1,2,3,1,2,3

text:
Installing fossick adds a fossick command. A shell script, or an agent with only a terminal, can use the library through it. The command takes a command name and then that command’s options:
Most commands wrap the Python function of the same name. Their options are that function’s arguments, with underscores written as hyphens: max_pages becomes --max-pages. A command offers only some of the function’s arguments. Output is readable markdown by default. --as-json prints JSON instead, for piping into other programs. paginate-api always prints JSON. fossick <command> --help lists a command’s options. fossick alone lists the commands.
Two defaults differ from Python. fossick search reranks with BM25 (--rerank lexical), and search in Python keeps the merged order. fossick search uses --region us-en, and search in Python uses region='auto'.

text:
Some pages need a login, a click on a button or a filled form before they show anything useful. A plain download cannot do this. This module drives a real Chrome through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), the interface that Chrome’s own developer tools use. It uses fastcdp for the connection.
The module uses one long-lived Chrome, which is separate from the Chrome you browse with. This debug Chrome listens for remote control on port 9223. It has its own profile, by default in ~/.cache/fastcdp/cdp-chrome. A site that you log in to in the debug Chrome stays logged in after a restart.
When a Chrome already listens on the port, cdp_connect and cdp_ws use it. The headless and extra_flags arguments then have no effect.
The functions in this module are async. Call them with await. In synchronous code, wrap them in syncy, as the examples do. Most of them are methods that this module adds to the CDP connection and Page classes of fastcdp. These Page methods are the main ones:

text:
Acting on a page
An agent needs to know what it can click or type into. The HTML of a full page is too long to read for that. snapshot builds a short text view from the accessibility tree, the description of the page that screen readers use. Each control becomes one line, [#id] role "name", such as [#42] button "Add to cart". The id is the number that Chrome gives the element. With interactive=False, snapshot also lists headings, forms and other landmarks.
type_text clears a field before it types. fastcdp’s fill_text adds to the text already in the field. click_settle clicks and then waits for the page to settle. It does not fail when a click on a single-page app does not navigate.
fill_form takes a dictionary of {label: value}. It finds each field by its visible label or name. It types into text fields and chooses options in drop-downs. When you pass submit, it then clicks the button or link with that name. It returns a new snapshot. It raises ValueError when no field matches a label, or when no button or link matches submit.

Screenshots and annotation
collect gathers screenshots while a person browses. It adds a small bar with a capture button and a done button to the page. Each press of capture takes a screenshot with the bar hidden.
collect stops when one of these happens:

The person presses done.
count screenshots have been taken.
tout seconds have passed.
The stop event is set.

With every_n, collect also takes a screenshot every every_n seconds without a button press. When you pass save_dir, collect saves each screenshot there as a PNG file named from prefix (by default the page title) and returns a list of (image, path) pairs. Without save_dir it returns a list of images.
BUTTON_JS, HIDE and SHOW are the scripts that draw, hide and show the bar.
